analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by all law enforcement and lets people sue to stop it.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan End Racial Profiling Act, with 95 House cosponsors including 8 Republicans, never left a House subcommittee and died without a floor vote when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for any law enforcement agency — federal, state, local, or tribal — to use race, ethnicity, or national origin to decide whom to stop, search, or question. People harmed could sue to stop the practice, federal agencies would have to adopt anti-profiling policies and collect stop data, and states would have to certify they had anti-profiling policies to keep certain federal police grants. The bill was introduced in June 2001, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Crime Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 107th Congress ended [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — especially Black and Hispanic drivers and residents — who are stopped, searched, or questioned because of their race rather than any specific suspicion. The bill's own findings cite Justice Department data showing Black and Hispanic drivers were more likely to be stopped and searched yet less likely to be carrying contraband than white drivers [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and residents stopped because of their race

how_it_helps.text: Bans racial profiling by every law enforcement agent and agency in the country, federal, state, local, and tribal [S3].
Lets the United States or an individual harmed by profiling sue in federal or state court for a court order ending the practice, with attorney's fees available to prevailing individuals [S2][S3].

Makes statistical proof enough to open a case: showing that routine stops and searches fall disproportionately on racial or ethnic minorities would count as prima facie evidence of a violation [S2][S3].

Requires federal agencies to adopt anti-profiling policies, collect data on stops and searches, handle complaints independently, and discipline officers who profile; state and local agencies must do the same as a condition of major federal police funding like the Byrne grants and the COPS program [S2][S3].

Funds training, data systems, dashboard cameras, and early-warning systems for departments, with a guaranteed share for small and rural agencies, and requires the Attorney General to report to Congress annually on profiling nationwide, with the collected data public [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies and the governments that run them: they would have to build data-collection and complaint systems, change how officers select whom to stop, face lawsuits, and risk losing federal grant money if they did not comply [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and the governments funding them

drawbacks.text: The bill made statistical disparity alone enough to establish a case — a lower bar than existing constitutional law, which generally requires proof that an officer intentionally used race. Police agencies argued this could penalize departments for enforcement patterns arising from factors other than officer bias [S3].

The compliance burden was real: departments would need new data systems, complaint procedures, and training, and grant conditions gave the Attorney General power to withhold Byrne, COPS, and local block grant funds from noncompliant agencies, which raised local-control objections [S3].

The definition of racial profiling covered reliance on race, ethnicity, or national origin 'to any degree' in stops, searches, and even immigration-related workplace investigations, a breadth that drew concern that legitimate investigations — including post-September 2001 immigration enforcement — could be constrained [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: the bill's own findings show profiling produces stops that yield contraband far less often than race-neutral searching would, so most of what it would stop is ineffective and humiliating [S3]. The genuine costs are administrative compliance and a legal standard broader than current constitutional law. Whether that trade is worth it was never tested — the House never debated the bill on the floor, so there was no amended version or public vote to weigh.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee's Crime Subcommittee from July 2001 until the Congress ended in January 2003, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Representative John Conyers, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill on June 6, 2001, joined by original cosponsors including Republicans Christopher Shays, Connie Morella, Jim Greenwood, Rodney Frelinghuysen, Mike Ferguson, and Jim Walsh — unusual bipartisan support for a civil-rights bill [S1][S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and to the Subcommittee on Crime on July 16, 2001 [S1][S5].

No further action was ever recorded; the bill was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never voted on in the House or Senate before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies and their unions benefited, since they avoided new anti-profiling mandates, data collection, liability, and grant conditions. Members of Congress who preferred not to cast a recorded vote on the issue also avoided one. The people the bill's findings showed were disproportionately stopped and searched — Black and Hispanic Americans — gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.role: Ranking Democrat, House Judiciary Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Racial Profiling Act on June 6, 2001 and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors [S1][S5].

for.name: 8 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including several original cosponsors at introduction [S3][S4].

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Joined Conyers as an original cosponsor at the bill's introduction [S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to and never reported from
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or a committee vote; it was referred to the full committee on June 6, 2001 and to the Subcommittee on Crime on July 16, 2001, and no further action was taken [S5].

against.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controlled whether the bill received a markup or floor consideration; the bill never advanced past subcommittee in his two years as chair.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor despite its 95 cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan in sponsorship — 86 of 208 House Democrats, 8 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent signed on — but the bill's death was controlled by the Republican-run committee and floor process, which took no action.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police unions
industries.note: The bill would have required departments to adopt anti-profiling policies, collect and publish stop data, discipline officers, and face lawsuits and grant cutoffs for noncompliance. Police groups opposed racial-profiling mandates as a data-collection and liability burden that second-guessed officers' split-second decisions. The public interest in unbiased policing ran against the agencies' interest in avoiding oversight.
